title: Aromatase activity in the neural tissues of the Canadian red-sided garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis) under hibernaculum temperatures

authors.affiliation: Department of Science, Saint Xavier University, 3700 W. 103rd Street, Chicago, IL 60655 USA

abstract_text: Numerous studies have indicated that the initiation of spring courtship behavior and mating in the male Canadian red-sided garter snake, unlike most vertebrate species, is independent of circulating androgens. Recently, however, field data has shown that circulating levels of testosterone (T), elevated in the fall, remain elevated throughout hibernation and upon emergence. Even though T levels are elevated in the spring, to date, the only known stimulus initiating courtship behavior is a period of low temperature dormancy followed by the onset of warm temperatures. In the field, winters (and subsequently hibernation) can begin as early as October and extend into May. In the laboratory, courtship behavior can be initiated after as few as seven weeks under hibernaculum conditions (total darkness at 4-5C). However, as the duration of the dormancy period was increased (up to 17 weeks) courtship behavior intensified. Similar to other vertebrates, the neural pathways critical for the initiation and maintenance of courtship behavior in the Canadian red-sided garter snake have been shown to contain sex steroid concentrating neurons. However, while these neurons respond to seasonal variations in T, the role of testosterone in the initiation and maintenance of courtship behavior in the male red-sided garter snake has continued to elude investigators. Recent studies have identified aromatase activity (AA) within specific areas of the pathway closely associated with the steroid concentrating neurons. The presence of AA within the areas controlling courtship suggests T may play an indirect role in "setting up" this neural pathway during the protracted hibernation in the field. This study was designed to investigate AA in neural tissues maintained under conditions of hibernation. To determine if AA was intensified in areas containing sex steroid concentrating neurons, areas associated with courtship behavior were isolated using a specific-area micro dissection punch technique. Specific areas investigated included the anterior-hypothalamus preoptic area (AHPOA), nucleus sphericus (NS), and the septum (S). Punches were taken from the cortex (C) as a possible control. There was no significant difference in AA in animals collected in the spring or fall. There was a significant overall gender difference in AA, with females exhibiting higher levels of AA in the AHPOA and NS. In males, the AHPOA and septum exhibited significantly greater AA than the nucleus sphericus and cortex, while the AHPOA exhibited significantly elevated AA when compared to the other neural areas.

title: Applied Herpetology: a new journal proposed

abstract_text: Applied amphibian and reptile research covers natural products development [toxinology (snake and lizard venoms), pharmacology (amphibian skin secretions), reptile leather and tortoiseshell industries]; environmental monitoring [amphibian teratology from incidence of abnormalities, and herpetofaunal ecotoxicology and contamination bioindicators]; farming [captive breeding and husbandry techniques for restocking populations, exhibition, teaching and experimentation], and conservation and wildlife management [species conservation, biodiversity assessment and sustainable utilization]. Papers in applied herpetology are often published in non-herpetological journals, or in the world's herpetological journals, which are in effect subsidising governmental, international agency and commercial sponsors of such work. There is a case for publication of peer-reviewed papers in applied research to be funded by these sponsors, especially since relatively little research in herpetology is now financed that is not applied. Such sponsors should include an allocation in projects proposed for the funding of publications.

title: Herpetofauna of the Albany Pine Bush

authors.affiliation: The University at Albany, Albany, New York

abstract_text: The Albany Pine Bush is a unique ecosystem characterized by sandy soils, vernal pools and pitch pine / scrub oak forests located in the towns of Colonie, Guilderland and the city of Albany, New York. Using historic and current data, Stewart and Rossi (1981) reported the presence of 30 species of herpetofauna in the Albany Pine Bush. Since that time, there has been a significant commercial and residential development in and around the Pine Bush. This study represents a re-survey of the area to determine what species of amphibians and reptiles are present today, estimate their relative abundance and draw on Stewart and Rossi's work to estimate the impact that 20 years of development has had upon the ecosystem and its inhabitants.

title: Food habits of the European wall lizard, Podarcis sicula, introduced to Long Island, New York

abstract_text: We studied the stomach contents of 150 European wall lizards, Podarcis sicula, collected from several populations in western Long Island, New York, throughout their active season in 1997. Their diets were made up of a wide variety of ants, insect larva, beetles, spiders, and millipedes. The list of prey included many introduced species. We compared our results to those reported for this species and conspecifics in their native habitat. We found a correlation between prey size and head width, which suggests that head width or a morphological factor associated with head width, may constrain the size of prey that individual lizards can consume. We further noted that some individuals had eaten several prey items of the same species, which is surprising in cases of prey species that do not normally congregate. This suggests that individual lizards may specialize on particular prey species, and actively forage for that species. We also tested for differences in food habits of males and females, independent of body size.

title: A comparison of the movements of indigenous and displaced long-term captive ornate box turtles (Terrapene ornata) in the Sand Hills of Nebraska

abstract_text: Herpetologists often release animals after laboratory study in a laudable attempt at conservation. However, the subsequent fates of such animals are generally unknown. We hypothesized that the behavior of these animals would be markedly altered, possibly compromising their survival. We compared movements of turtles, captured in the field and fitted with thread-trailers, with a matched group released simultaneously after one year of captivity. We trailed each animal for 200 m (two or three days) and we subsequently mapped these trails, computing for each the minimum convex polygon area, the maximum recorded speed, and three measures of trail sinuosity (the square root of area divided by trail length (L), the greatest distance between two points divided by L, and the fractal dimension (D)). The variance of the captive turtle data was significantly greater than that for the native turtles for trail area and for two of the three sinuosity measures. However, contrary to expectations, none of the mean values differed significantly between these groups, nor were there any obvious trends. Although we have no survivorship data, long-term captivity and release in an unfamiliar location does not appear to markedly affect the short-term movement patterns of ornate box turtles.

title: Scales of diversity: the role of parks in conserving genetic population structure of threatened snakes

abstract_text: We used DNA sampled from black rat snakes (Elaphe o. obsoleta) and eastern massasauga rattlesnakes (Sistrurus c. catenatus) in Ontario to investigate genetic population structure at several spatial scales. Our findings based on RAPD markers indicate that geographically-isolated populations of rat snakes may not be genetically distinct, and that sub-structuring within regional populations might be attributable to reduced snake movement and gene flow due to ecological barriers. As such, park agencies should develop cooperative management strategies for regional populations that span multiple jurisdictions. Data from microsatellite markers indicate that isolated massasauga populations are highly divergent and that regional populations may be comprised of inbred local populations. Thus, fine-scale genetic structuring may be the norm for massasauga populations, rather than a consequence of recent (< 300 years) anthropogenic effects. These data support the view that individual populations of massasaugas associated with parks have high conservation genetic value since many populations probably contain a unique portion of sub-specific variation. This research has helped direct conservation efforts by providing parks with a means of assessing the relative distinctiveness of remnant populations, an empirical basis for identifying appropriate scales of management, and a method for testing the efficacy of conservation actions.

abstract_text: We collected European wall lizards, Podarcis sicula, from separate but similar populations in western Long Island, New York, throughout the spring and summer of 1997, and assessed their reproductive condition. title: Cross-species amplification of microsatellites developed for timber rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus)

abstract_text: Microsatellite analysis is a useful tool in studies of population genetics and kinship; however, few microsatellite loci have been isolated for use with snake species. title: Origins of the American snake fauna

authors.affiliation: Rendalia Biologists, Talladega, AL 35160

abstract_text: Recent geological, paleontological, morphological, and molecular studies provide identification and better definitions of the diverse clades that comprise the present American snake fauna. No single field provides a clear zoogeographic narrative of these faunal elements but the consilience of information from multiple sources offers such a base. Not unexpectedly, the oldest surviving clades are also the most ancient ones in the Americas. The typhlopids and leptotyphlopids of the Neotropics and Africa probably date from the mid-Cretaceous splitting of Gondwana by the Atlantic Ocean. The anomalepedids and Anilius in contrast are ancient South American endemics without known relatives, although the latter may be a Recent relative of the Cretaceous +Dinilysia. The Neotropical (true) boids appear to represent an ancient henophidian fauna that ranged from Madagascar across Antarctica to South America. Conversely, the American erycids, tropidophiids (and ?ungaliophiids and ?Loxocemus) derive from the Cretaceous-to-Eocene connection of eastern North America with Europe. This also may be true of the caenophidian "North American Relicts." The main American caenophidian fauna (crotalids, elapids, xenodontids, dipsadids, colubrids s.s., and natricids) did not arrive until later. Both paleontological and molecular data support two or more Miocene entries of these snakes from the Old World via Bering Strait.

abstract_text: The angle-headed dragons, Gonocephalus sensu lato have often been given as an example of a vertebrate that straddles Wallace's Line. abstract_text: In an attempt to establish the outgroup of the genus Cacosternum Boulenger 1887, a preliminary molecular investigation into the relationships among the genera of the sub-family Petropedetinae was conducted. abstract_text: In a field study on 11 Boiga irregularis, propofol provided 15-20 minutes of surgical anesthesia. abstract_text: We assessed European wall lizards, Podarcis sicula, collected from populations introduced to the U.S., for the ability to tolerate freezing temperatures. abstract_text: Correlations between breeding date and the life history or energy stores of individuals might arise owing to two different mechanisms: condition dependence or adaptation-by-time. These values are far in excess of the number of snakes typically found in a single hibernaculum and suggest relatively large genetic neighborhoods encompassing many communal hibernacula. Our results suggest viscosity of gene flow over relatively short distances (at the scale of tens of kilometers) but substantial genetic exchange among local hibernacula.

title: Studies of lung-based hearing in amphibians and reptiles

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, Ohio State University, 1735 Neil Avenue, Columbus, OH 43210-1293 USA

abstract_text: Lungs have been shown to function in reception of airborne sound in snakes and species of frogs that lack tympanic middle ears, and this lung pathway may represent the most primitive mechanism of hearing in tetrapod vertebrates. Laser vibrometric studies were extended to investigate the acoustic responsiveness of the lateral body walls and lungs of salamanders and lizards, and additional studies analyzing potential routes of sound energy transfer from the lungs to the inner ear were conducted on frogs. The body walls of several species of salamanders and lizards were found to be responsive to sound, typically showing a low frequency peak in motion (< 300 Hz) and a higher frequency peak from 800-2000 Hz depending on body size. In contrast, the body wall of lungless plethodontid salamanders showed a reduced low frequency peak in motion and completely lacked the higher frequency peak. Neurophysiological studies on fire-bellied toads (Bombina orientalis) suggest that sound energy is not transferred from the lung to the inner ear via respiratory pathways. Vibrometric experiments suggest instead that the opercularis system may be involved. Sound-induced motion of the suprascapula decreased dramatically when sound was blocked from reaching the body wall/lung. Lung-induced motion of the suprascapula may be relayed via the opercularis muscle to the operculum in the oval window of the inner ear.

title: A new look at what the eye implies about the early ancestors of snakes

authors.affiliation: Evolution, Ecology, and Organismal Biology, Ohio State University, 1735 Neil Avenue, Columbus, OH 43210 USA

abstract_text: Gordon Walls (1940, 1942) constructed an elegant, logical story for the early origin of snakes as burrowers, based upon the anatomy of the eye. Independently, Mahendra (1938) suggested that burrowing snakes, such as Typhlops, represented the most basal snake lineages, also underscoring the hypothesis of a fossorial ancestry for snakes. This hypothesis, with some modification, has been widely accepted (Underwood, 1970; Rieppel, 1988). Recent phylogenetic research by Caldwell and Lee (1997) suggested an alternative to the fossorial ancestor hypothesis, reviving an early hypothesis for an aquatic origin of modern snakes. Can the ophthalmic characteristics so forcefully argued by Walls for a fossorial origin of snakes equally support an argument for an aquatic origin for snakes? In fact, many of these same ophthalmic characteristics are observed in aquatic taxa. The shape and relative size of the lens and the method of accommodation in modern snakes are typical of aquatic animals and suggest an aquatic ancestry for snakes. Other characteristics of the eye are less obviously attributable to an aquatic ancestor but are still consistent with this alternative hypothesis. In light of the revised historical framework, this alternative hypothesis for the ecological origin for snakes merits closer inspection.

title: Evaluation of a by-catch reduction device to reduce diamondback terrapin (Malaclemys terrapin) mortality in crab pots

authors.affiliation: Ohio University, Athens, OH, USA
Dept. of Biological Sciences, Ohio University, Athens, OH 45701 USA

abstract_text: Diamondback terrapins, Malaclemys terrapin, frequently drown due to incidental capture in crab pots. Crab pots selectively capture male and young female terrapins, thereby skewing sex ratios and removing individuals with high reproductive value. We tested a by-catch reduction device (BRD) to determine its ability to reduce terrapin entrapment and the effect the BRD had on the size and number of crabs that were caught in crab pots. We tested three size BRDs, 4 cm x 10 cm, 4.5 cm x 12 cm and 5 cm x 10 cm, on both standard crab pots and modified crab pots designed to prevent terrapin mortality. We found that the 4 cm x 10 cm BRD effectively prevented turtle entry, however, eliminated crabs based on height. Neither the 5 cm x 10 cm nor the 4.5 cm x 12 cm BRDs affected crab size or the number of crabs caught, but the 4.5 cm x 12 cm BRD reduced terrapin by-catch by 82 percent, whereas the 5 cm x 10 cm BRD only reduced terrapin by-catch by 50%. We stress the importance of using BRDs to reduce terrapin captures throughout their range, thus preserving the biodiversity of wetland ecosystems and restoring or maintaining natural sex ratios of terrapin populations.

title: Estimating gopher tortoise population sizes: Management implications of a study in South Carolina

authors.affiliation: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, University of Georgia, P.O. Drawer E, Aiken, SC 29802, USA
Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, University of Georgia, P.O. Drawer E, Aiken, SC 29802, USA

abstract_text: The gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) is legally protected by state regulations throughout its range and federally listed as threatened in the western portion of its range. Population sizes of gopher tortoises have traditionally been calculated using standard correction factors that estimate the number of tortoises based on the number of burrows in a given area. However, correction factors may vary among seasons, habitats, and regions and there are no quantitative studies on gopher tortoises in the northeastern portion their range. We used a volunteer-based burrow count survey to mark 1174 potential tortoise burrows on the Tillman Sand Ridge Heritage Preserve in Jasper County, SC. To evaluate the effectiveness of the burrow count survey for estimating tortoise population size, we investigated 368 marked burrows using infrared burrow cameras. We observed 49 tortoises using the burrow cameras and estimated the population size to be 153 adult tortoises. Our site-specific correction of 0.183 is considerably lower than previously published correction factors and resulted in a substantially lower population estimate than those calculated from widely used correction factors. Our results emphasize the critical need to consider regional variation in the relationship between burrow number and tortoise population size when developing and using correction factors.

title: On conservation of the Sahelian giant tortoise, Geochelone sulcata

authors.affiliation: Environmental Sciences Department, Natural Resources Institute (University of Greenwich), Central Avenue, Chatham Maritime, Kent ME4 4TB, England

abstract_text: Geochelone sulcata (Cryptodira: Testudinidae) achieves a length of 830 mm and weight of 105.5 kg, and is the largest of the world's continental tortoises. It has a range forming a 600-700 km wide belt across Africa's Sahelian region from Mauritania and Senegal in the west to Eritrea and Ethiopia in the east, and was reported still to be common in the western Sahel during the late 19th century. The information database is poor, but populations today are known to be very depleted in most of the range, due to utilization as food by local people and collection for the international live animal trade. The giant tortoise inhabits light savannah woodland, grassy during June-October rains, but sparsely vegetated and livestock-trampled during the Sahelian dry season. Refuge is sought in burrows. The species occurs in zones with mean annual rainfall 140-1098 mm. The bioclimatic range is "desertic", "sub-desertic" and barely "warm tropical - dry season of long duration", and vegetation mainly "Semi-desert grassland and shrubland: northern Sahel and Somalia-Masai", "Sahel Acacia woodland, grassland and deciduous bushland" and "undifferentiated woodland: Sudanian and Ethiopian". Using locality records, a project is being developed to map the giant tortoise's optimum habitat by means of satellite imagery. This will form the basis for recommending the creation of a natural reserve in Mali, and areas for re-stocking with captive-bred animals.

title: Ecology of the Jamaican slider turtle (Trachemys terrapen), with implications for conservation and management

authors.affiliation: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, University of Georgia, SC, 29802, USA
Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, University of Georgia, SC, 29802, USA
Institute of Ecology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA 30602, USA
Institute of Ecology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA 30602, USA

abstract_text: We investigated populations of the Jamaican slider turtle (Trachemys terrapen), a species endemic to Jamaica. We sampled turtles at four sites - three along the southern Jamaican coast and one in northwest Jamaica. We captured turtles in a variety of habitats, including a permanently ponded wetland, farm ponds, and a stream in a karst landscape. Turtles were also found in a series of seasonal ponds where they retreat into nearby cave refugia. The refugia remain flooded, thus allowing the slider population to exist in this seasonally arid landscape. We did not observe or capture turtles during limited sampling in a large river and a brackish mangrove swamp. Individuals from the northwest population appeared morphologically distinct from turtles captured along the south coast and descriptions of T. terrapen provided in the literature. The native people harvest turtles whenever they are found incidentally. Concentrated populations, such as those in the cave refugia, are heavily exploited. We found red-eared sliders (Trachemys scripta elegans) in Jamaican pet stores and suspect they could become established in Jamaica, possibly hybridizing with the native slider. Our preliminary research suggests that T. terrapen is a highly threatened species needing conservation action in order to insure its persistence.

title: A comparison of morphological and reproductive characteristics of nesting loggerhead sea turtle populations

authors.affiliation: Archie Carr Center for Sea Turtle Research, 223 Bartram Hall, Dept. of Zoology, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611
Archie Carr Center for Sea Turtle Research, 223 Bartram Hall, Dept. of Zoology, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611

abstract_text: Few studies have addressed intraspecific trends within a marine turtle species over a large area. The main objective of this study was to quantify whether loggerhead sea turtles nesting in Florida, Brazil, and Greece differ significantly in their morphology and reproductive output. Data on body size, clutch size and egg size were collected from nesting females. To place ideas in a more general perspective, morphological and reproductive data on other loggerhead populations were compiled from the literature and examined for latitudinal trends within the Atlantic and Mediterranean. Differences in morphology and reproductive output were observed among the three populations, indicating that each population experiences and responds to a unique combination of factors both at and away from the nesting beach. Both body size and egg size were significantly correlated with latitude. However, correlations were not significant when Mediterranean data were excluded, suggesting that turtles in the Mediterranean encounter environmental conditions significantly different from oceanic populations. This study highlights important differences among populations, broadens the concept of life history variation to a turtle species not confined to a single geographic location, and emphasizes the need for conserving genetic and phenotypic variation in marine turtle populations.

title: Effects of human disturbance on five-lined skink (Eumeces fasciatus) abundance and distribution at Point Pelee National Park, Canada

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, ON, N1G 2W1
Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, ON, N1G 2W1
Department of Biological Sciences, University of Windsor, Windsor, ON, N9B 3P4

abstract_text: The five-lined skink is widely distributed in eastern North America but its populations are disjunct and of conservation concern in the northern portion of its range. Canadian populations are presently considered "vulnerable". We studied effects of human disturbance on five-lined skinks at Point Pelee National Park, from 1990 to 1997. Surveys indicated low skink abundance and a lack of woody debris in areas heavily used by humans. A population decline, concurrent with high disturbance levels, occurred from 1990 to 1996. Skinks used woody debris as refuge sites and showed preferential use of large moderately decayed logs and boards having greater surface area. Human disturbance resulted in degradation and removal of debris. To test the hypothesis that skink absence in human high-use areas was caused by a lack of suitable debris, we placed artificial microhabitats in areas which previously lacked debris and skinks. Experimental boards were quickly colonized and heavily used despite high disturbance rates. Results suggested that skinks are resilient to minor disturbances such as board displacements, but not to removal or degradation of debris. Habitat restoration by moving large woody debris from open beach to the stabilized dune began in 1996 and resulted in increased skink abundance in 1997.

title: The effects of road mortality on two threatened snake species on Pelee Island, Ontario

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1
Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1
Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1

abstract_text: Road mortality is becoming an increasing threat to endangered and isolated reptile populations. Reptiles killed by motorized vehicles and found on Pelee Island's roads (68 km in total) were collected and locations recorded from 1993-1996. During the three years of intense surveys, the roads were scanned approximately every two days. In 1998, sections of road that had high numbers of roadkilled blue racers (Coluber constrictor foxii) and eastern fox snakes (Elaphe gloydi) during the roadkill surveys, will be scanned intensively to determine suitable methods to mitigate the effects of vehicular mortality. The blue racer is endangered in Canada, and threatened status for the eastern fox snake is pending review. In three years 78 blue racers (11 adults/year) and greater than 100 eastern fox snakes were found dead on Pelee Island's roads. Many adult females that are killed on the roads are moving to or from shoreline oviposition sites. In the fall of each year, many hatchlings are also found dead on the roads. For example, from 1993-1996, 75 hatchling eastern fox snakes were recorded as roadkills. As a result of continuing development in the form of summer cottages, and growing tourism, vehicular traffic continues to increase on Pelee Island's roads. The future impact of increased traffic flow and continued road mortality on the blue racer and eastern fox snake remains to be seen. Our data suggest that road mortality will be a significant factor leading to the decline of both snake species on Pelee Island.

title: The impact of roads on snake populations in eastern Texas

authors.affiliation: Southern Research Station, Box 7600, SFA Station, Nacogdoches, TX 75962 USA
Southern Research Station, Box 7600, SFA Station, Nacogdoches, TX 75962 USA
Southern Research Station, Box 7600, SFA Station, Nacogdoches, TX 75962 USA
Southern Research Station, Box 7600, SFA Station, Nacogdoches, TX 75962 USA

abstract_text: Radio-telemetry studies of timber rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus) and Louisiana pine snakes (Pituophis ruthveni) suggested that mortality associated with roads was a significant factor in the biology of these species. An analysis of timber rattlesnake records in relation to road densities supported the hypothesis that mortality associated with roads has resulted in the extirpation of this species from significant portions of the landscape. The hypothesis that existing road networks depress populations of large snake species was tested using a trapping protocol to sample snake populations up to 850 m from road corridors. Preliminary results suggest that snake populations are reduced by 50% or more up to a distance of 450 m from roads with moderate use. There was no indication that the population indices had reached an asymptote at a distance of 850 m. For some species the data suggest that larger individuals are located further from road corridors. Quantification of the road network on a landscape scale indicates that the large snake fauna of eastern Texas is subject to significant road related mortality that has the potential to reduce populations by 50% or more across a large proportion of the landscape.

title: Habitat use, home ranges and hibernacula of the copperbelly water snake (Nerodia erythrogaster neglecta) in southern Indiana and northwest Kentucky

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Indiana-Purdue University, Ft. Wayne, IN 46805 USA
Department of Biology, Indiana-Purdue University, Ft. Wayne, IN 46805 USA

abstract_text: The copperbelly is federally listed under the Endangered Species Act as Threatened in the northern part of its range, and protected to the south by the Copperbelly Water Snake Conservation Agreement. Snakes from two populations were radio-tracked at the Sloughs Wildlife Management Area, Kentucky, and in the Patoka National Wildlife Refuge, Indiana. The movements of the snakes were monitored to elucidate patterns of home range size and habitat use, including hibernacula sites. Habitat use was seasonally compared between sexes. Home ranges and activity centers were calculated using minimum convex polygons. Individual snakes occupied widely different habitats, demonstrated pronounced fidelity to selected habitats for much of the season. Buttonbush sloughs and areas of shallow water with emergent vegetation were most frequently used, while closed canopy forested habitats away from the sloughs and large bodies of open water were not. Habitat use shifted towards palustrine forest edges as the season progressed. The hibernacula of most snakes were crayfish burrows or stumps near or within the floodplain.

title: Conservation of the endangered copperbelly water snake, Nerodia erythrogaster neglecta

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Indiana-Purdue University, Fort Wayne, IN 46805 USA

abstract_text: The copperbelly is an inhabitant of shallow wetlands in parts of the midwestern United States. It is state listed as Endangered by Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio, federally listed as Threatened to the north by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, and protected in southern Indiana, southern Illinois, and Kentucky by a conservation agreement. Over the last few years, efforts have dramatically increased to learn more about the species' ecological requirements to prevent further losses of snakes or suitable habitat. I will review efforts to conserve the remaining populations of the copperbelly. Discussion will include a review of the current status of the snake, both in the legal and biological senses, and a description of the conservation agreement. I will also examine the implications of research findings from several studies out of my lab regarding management decisions about restoring and reclaiming habitat for the species.

title: Long-term changes in movement patterns of massasauga rattlesnakes following a severe flood

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana Univ., Hammond, LA 70402-0736 USA
Dept. of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana Univ., Hammond, LA 70402-0736 USA

abstract_text: From 1979-1983 we conducted radiotelemetry and mark-recapture studies on massasauga rattlesnakes (Sistrurus catenatus) at the Squaw Creek National Wildlife Refuge in northwestern Missouri. These data showed that snakes hibernated in a moist prairie, moved away from the prairie to drier areas in the late spring and summer, and returned to the prairie in the fall. In 1993, the refuge was impacted severely by the "Great Midwestern Flood"; massasauga populations showed significant changes in population size structure, sex ratio, mass-length relationships, and reproduction as a result of this event. From 1996-1997 we re-examined the movement patterns of this population to determine any additional effects of the flood. We found that although snakes still hibernate in the main prairie, very few massasaugas leave the prairie for outlying areas, but remain in the prairie during the summer. In addition, the number of massasaugas found crossing roads on the refuge has decreased dramatically, and the snakes that do cross refuge roads are mainly neonates rather than adults as was seen in the earlier study. The implications for these apparent changes in movement patterns for management and conservation will be discussed.

title: Amphibians, reptiles, and phosphate mining in Florida

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology and Center for Urban Ecology, University of South Florida, Tampa, Florida 33620, USA
Department of Biology and Center for Urban Ecology, University of South Florida, Tampa, Florida 33620, USA

abstract_text: Much of central Florida has been subjected to strip mining for phosphate. The mining process drastically alters the upland habitats available for wildlife occupancy. We collected amphibians and reptiles at 30 unmined xeric upland sites and 30 previously mined sites to determine which amphibians and reptiles may be under-represented at the reclaimed mined sites. Thirteen species of amphibians (4) and reptiles (9) were determined to be "focal species," that is, they were under-represented at the reclaimed mine sites, relative to the unmined sites. Reasons for their under-representation include the lack of suitable substrate for burrowing species, lack of temporary ponds for amphibian reproduction, and lack of sufficient litter, ground cover, and plant structure for other species. Plans to further study selected focal species, including translocating common species to reclaimed habitats will be reviewed.

title: [title illegible in scan - Great Basin fishes: rates of differentiation, speciation, and extinction (Hubbs and Miller legacy)]

authors.affiliation: Museum of Zoology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

abstract_text: Hubbs and Miller's research on the Great Basin emphasized changes at the level of races and subspecies; these changes apparently occurred rapidly, in hundreds to thousands of years. Miocene to Pleistocene fossils of these fishes, in contrast, suggest unexpectedly slow changes at the species level, i.e., over hundreds of thousands to nearly 10 million years, with infrequent evolution of new species. Resolution of this incongruence requires clarification of the relative frequency of short-term differentiation, species origins, and extinction. The Great Basin evidence demonstrates that fluctuating pluvial-interpluvial cycles result in rapid proliferation of new subspecies but eventual extinction of all but generalist survivors, often as relict endemics. The frequent extinctions and infrequent persistence of new species in the Great Basin seem to be the consequence of repeated loss of habitat during interpluvial stages of Pleistocene cycles. The result seems to be rapid but superficial changes in morphology without long-term change. Great Basin fish faunas exhibit low diversity and high endemism characteristic of tectonically active areas. The low diversity suggests that high extinction rates were caused by high elevations, high gradients (low habitat diversity), and climatic variability.
